# My Playbook for ref_estate

**On purchasing properties:**
When I land on an unowned property, I buy it if I have the cash available. Properties generate rent income and contribute to my final score, so early acquisition builds my portfolio. Don't overthink it—if I can afford it, I should own it. This game confirmed it: I bought Wharf and Exchange early, and they paid me 60 in rent by lap 3, which funded my ability to stay competitive.

**On affording purchases:**
When I cannot afford a property outright, I decline without hesitation. Negative cash is not an option. However, I can afford to go lower on cash reserves than I initially thought—spending down to zero (Exchange purchase) or near-zero (Terrace purchase at 9 cash) is acceptable if it secures properties, because rent income will rebuild my reserves.

**On paying rent:**
When I land on an opponent's property, I pay the rent owed immediately and accurately. Track my cash carefully: last declared balance + any transfers received - rent owed = new balance. Don't make arithmetic errors here.

**On passing START:**
When I pass START, I collect my salary. This is free cash—always account for it in my balance update. Every pass is money I should be adding to my reserves.

**On properties I own:**
When I land on a property I own, nothing happens. I owe no rent and cannot buy it again. Move on.

**On final lap strategy:**
In the final lap, even if my cash reserves are minimal, I should still buy unowned properties if I can afford them. The game ends immediately after lap 6, so there are no future turns where I'll regret being cash-poor. Owning one more deed in the final scoring is worth the liquidity hit.

**On strategy going forward:**
Aggressively acquire properties throughout all laps, especially high-rent properties like Exchange and Mill. Rent income compounds—the sooner I own properties, the longer they work for me. I should not hoard cash; cash sitting idle is inefficient. The winning metric is total portfolio value plus remaining cash at the end, so properties are as good as reserves. Buy whenever I can, all the way through lap 6.

# My Playbook for ref_estate

**On each turn, calculate my true cash position first.** Declare what I paid this turn and what I now hold, keeping my own careful books. The scoring uses my declared balance plus my deed values, so accuracy matters. Always account for salary collected and rent received from other players since my last declared balance.

**When I land on an unowned property, evaluate it against my current cash and my position in the game.** Early in the game (laps 1-2), be willing to buy mid-tier properties (price 70-100) if I have solid cash reserves above 150. This builds my deed portfolio and generates income through rent. As the game progresses (laps 3-6), become more selective—only buy if I have sufficient cash cushion remaining (at least 50-60) after purchase. Late-game property grabs are less valuable since there are fewer turns left to recoup the investment.

**When I land on someone else's property, pay the rent immediately without hesitation.** This is inevitable and expected; don't waste mental energy on it. Ensure my cash calculation includes any incoming rent I've collected before calculating what I owe outgoing.

**Recognize that early property acquisition is valuable but must be balanced against cash preservation.** In this game, I held only one property (Foundry) throughout all 6 laps. Investor 0 accumulated multiple properties (Wharf, Exchange, Terrace) and likely scored higher. I should have bought more properties in laps 1-3 when I had better cash positions. A second or third property would have significantly increased my final score.

**When I have borderline cash for a property purchase, do the math clearly.** If a property costs more than half my current cash, buying it leaves me vulnerable to being broke if I land on expensive properties. Aim to keep at least 40-50 cash after any purchase to maintain flexibility.

**At START, always collect my salary.** This is free money each lap; treat it as part of my usable balance and include it in my calculations immediately.

**Track what other investors own and what properties are still available.** After each lap, note which properties have been bought and by whom. This tells me which tiles are still open for acquisition and which generate income for opponents. Properties that will generate frequent rent for others are less attractive to land on; prioritize buying available properties before they're locked up.

**By the final two laps, focus on cash preservation and accurate accounting.** Very few new property acquisitions happen this late. Document my final balance accurately, as the game is decided by cumulative declared cash plus deed value. A single property held through to the end (like my Foundry) contributes its purchase price to my final score.

**When deciding between two equally viable purchases, prefer higher-rent properties.** A property that generates 24 rent is better than one generating 12, all else equal, because other players will pay me more frequently over the remaining laps.

# Playbook for ref_estate

## Property Acquisition Strategy

When you land on an unowned property, buy it if you have sufficient cash and it generates reasonable rent relative to its cost. Properties with rent-to-cost ratios around 20-25% (like Wharf at 80/18 and Foundry at 100/24) are solid early investments.

Buy properties early in the game when you have capital available, as rental income compounds across laps and other players will visit your properties multiple times.

However, be selective about which properties to buy. In my last game, I bought Mill (90/20) on lap 3 and it was my only property purchase—this left me highly exposed to rent payments from other players' properties while generating minimal return. I finished with only 27 cash plus 90 in property value, for a total score of 117.

When you cannot afford a property you land on, simply decline and move on—do not overextend your cash reserves trying to force purchases you cannot make.

## Cash Management

Maintain a minimum cash buffer even after purchases. Do not spend your entire balance on property acquisition, as you need reserves for unexpected rent payments and to continue playing effectively.

Track your running balance carefully: account for salary collected when passing START, all rent received from other players, and all rent you owe when landing on opponents' properties.

Recognize that cash drain from paying rent to other players is a major threat. In my last game, I paid 24 + 30 + 24 + 30 = 108 in rent across 6 laps while collecting only 25 in salary. This created steady downward pressure on my cash reserves.

## Ownership Strategy

Acquiring multiple properties is critical to competitive scoring, not just one. Owning 2-3 properties creates a strong defensive position where incoming rent from opponents offsets the rent you must pay them.

Prioritize acquiring a second property to generate rental income streams. The early opportunities (like Quarry at 60/12, Wharf at 80/18, or Depot at 50/10) should be taken when available, even if they have lower rent-to-cost ratios.

## Late-Game Decisions

In the final laps, continue acquiring unowned properties when cash permits. Even properties with lower rent (like Depot at 50/10) become valuable in endgame because other players will land on them during the final lap(s), generating immediate revenue.

Prioritize maintaining positive cash flow and owning multiple properties over hoarding cash, since your final score is cash plus the purchase price of all deeds you hold.
